name: Wok hei — the breath of the wok
scope: Why a restaurant stir-fry tastes smoky-charred in a way a home pan can't match. T1: a wok is round-bottomed so food slides to a screaming-hot center and up the cooler sides — you toss constantly so nothing sits and steams. T2: a carbon-steel wok builds a black non-stick 'seasoning' patina from oil polymerizing onto the metal over time. T2: crowding the wok is the enemy — pile in too much and the pan cools, so food STEAMS grey instead of searing (dry heat browns, wet heat doesn't). T3: 'wok hei' (breath of the wok) is a distinct smoky aroma — not from charcoal but from the food and oil searing at ferocious heat. T3: the browning is the Maillard reaction — amino acids plus sugars rearranging into hundreds of roasty flavor compounds (same reaction that browns toast and seared steak). T4: the signature smokiness comes from the OIL: near 300C+ droplets aerosolize into a mist that briefly ignites over the flame and settles back onto the food as toasted-oil flavor. T5: home stoves rarely get hot enough — a restaurant wok burner roars at many times a home stove's output, which is why 'wok hei' is so hard to fake at home. T5: it stops just short of burning — the char flavor arrives while the food itself stays tender, a razor's-edge of heat and timing.
source: Grokipedia grokipedia.com/page/Wok_hei checked first (page exists; WebFetch 403-blocked) — corroborated via headcountcoffee.com 'The Science Behind Stir-Frying', misterwok.net/journal/wok-hei-physics, woksoflove.com 'How to Get Wok Hei at Home', ricebowldeluxe.com; Maillard reaction (general food-science consensus).
framing_note: Scene-led from the smoky restaurant plate; make the KNOWABLE cause the answer. Accuracy rail: wok hei is oil-aerosol combustion + Maillard, NOT charcoal smoke and NOT 'burnt' — it stops just short of char. Prep-voice ('you toss it over the flame') is fine. Payoff rung is T4 (the oil catches fire mid-air and rains flavor back onto the food).

name: Malà — Sichuan's numbing pepper
scope: The 'other' spicy — why Sichuan food buzzes as well as burns. T1: Sichuan cooking has TWO sensations, not one — a chili burn (là) AND a strange tingling numbness (má); together they're called málà. T2: the numbness comes from the Sichuan peppercorn, which despite its name is not a chili and not related to black pepper — it's the dried husk of a fruit in the CITRUS family (Zanthoxylum). T3: it doesn't hit heat/pain nerves like chili does — it fools your TOUCH nerves, so your lips feel like they're lightly vibrating or fluttering (the compound is sanshool; the buzz clocks near 50 taps a second). T4: cooks pair the numbing pepper WITH chili on purpose — the numbness dulls the mouth just enough that you can enjoy more chili heat without being overwhelmed. T5: this doubled sensation is the backbone of the classic dishes — mapo tofu and Chongqing hotpot are built on málà oil.
source: Grokipedia checked first — corroborated via en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sichuan_pepper, en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydroxy-%CE%B1-sanshool, smithsonianmag.com 'Why Szechuan Peppers Make Your Lips Go Numb', 50hertzfoods.com on málà.
framing_note: Invert the wonder: lead with the buzzing-lips sensation, make the citrus-family husk the answer. Accuracy rails: Sichuan pepper is NOT a chili or a true peppercorn (it's a Zanthoxylum husk), and it acts on TOUCH nerves not heat receptors; the '~50 taps a second' stays CONTEXT, never the tested answer (no bare number as answer). The chili half is New World — see the chili-into-Asia ladder. Payoff rung is T2 (it's a citrus relative, not pepper at all).

name: Chili's journey into Asia (the Columbian Exchange)
scope: The fiery red of Asian food is a plot twist only ~400 years old. T1: a chili's burn isn't heat at all — it's capsaicin, a chemical that tricks the same nerves that sense scalding, so your brain thinks your mouth is hot. T2: chili peppers are a NEW WORLD plant — domesticated in the Americas (Mexico and the Andes) and completely unknown in Asia before Columbus. T2: Portuguese traders carried chili around Africa to India and East Asia in the 1500s (part of the Columbian Exchange). T3: before chili arrived, 'spicy' Sichuan food leaned on the numbing Sichuan pepper plus ginger and mustard — the fiery-red identity we picture is barely 300 years old (Hunan first records chili in 1684). T3: Korea folded chili into kimchi and gochujang only after ~1600 — older kimchi was white and non-spicy. T4: most of a chili's heat lives in the white inner rib/pith, NOT the seeds as people assume; that heat is measured on the Scoville scale. T4: birds feel no burn from capsaicin and spread the seeds far and wide — the plant 'aims' its heat at seed-crushing mammals, so the burn is really a defense. T5: because capsaicin binds the body's real heat-sensor (TRPV1), your brain literally can't tell chili from a burn — the endorphin rush afterward is why people crave it. T5: chili tolerance is learned, not inborn — enjoying pain-that-can't-hurt-you is sometimes called 'benign masochism.'
source: Grokipedia checked first — corroborated via en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chili_pepper, thebeijinger.com 'How the Beloved Chili Arrived in China', scmp.com 'How Asians embraced the chilli pepper', splendidtable.org 'How chili peppers conquered the world'; capsaicin/TRPV1 pharmacology (general consensus).
framing_note: Food-driven history where the CHILI itself is always the anchor (no bare trade policy). Flagship accuracy rail: chili is a New World plant unknown in Asia before ~1500 — 'Asian food was always fiery-red' is FALSE (Portuguese carried it east in the 1500s; Hunan 1684, Sichuan ~1749). Attribute domestication to the Americas. Dates/Scoville numbers are context, never the tested answer. Payoff rung is T4 (birds feel no burn and spread the seeds — the heat is aimed at mammals).

name: Dashi and the discovery of umami
scope: The savory base under nearly all Japanese cooking — and the taste it revealed. T1: dashi is the clear broth beneath miso soup and countless Japanese dishes — made simply from kombu (kelp) and shavings of dried fish (bonito, katsuobushi). T1: it delivers a deep savory, mouth-filling taste that isn't salty, sweet, sour, or bitter. T2: that taste is umami, now recognized as the fifth basic taste; the kelp supplies it through glutamate (an amino acid). T3: in 1908 the chemist Kikunae Ikeda isolated glutamate from kombu and named the taste umami ('pleasant savory taste'). T3: bonito flakes bring a SECOND savory molecule, inosinate, from the fish. T4: glutamate and inosinate together taste far MORE savory than either alone — 'umami synergy' multiplies rather than adds, which is exactly why the kombu-plus-bonito pairing became the classic. T4: the same glutamate is naturally rich in parmesan, ripe tomatoes, mushrooms, and cured ham — which is why those foods taste 'savory' the world over. T5: MSG is simply that same glutamate isolated as a salt — the identical molecule found in kombu and tomato; the mid-century scare that blamed it for illness was never substantiated. T5: katsuobushi is among the hardest foods on earth — bonito that's smoked, dried, and mold-fermented into a wood-like block, then shaved paper-thin.
source: Grokipedia checked first — corroborated via umamiinfo.com 'What is Dashi'/'What is Umami', en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kikunae_Ikeda, ajinomoto.com 'Who Identified Umami and When', ice.edu 'How Dashi Led to the Discovery of MSG', ramenchemistry.com 'Umami Synergy'.
framing_note: Scene-led from a bowl of miso soup and that 'savory-but-not-salty' puzzle. Accuracy rails: Ikeda IDENTIFIED and NAMED umami in 1908 (do not say he 'invented' the taste); MSG is the SAME glutamate found in kombu, tomato, and parmesan and the old scare was never substantiated (settled nutrition, not a contested stance). BANNED: the tested answer is never the exact 1:1 ratio or a Latin name — teach the concept (kelp gives glutamate, fish gives inosinate, together they multiply). Payoff rung is T4 (the two-molecule synergy / the same glutamate hides in parmesan and tomato).

name: Sushi: from preservation to nigiri
scope: The surprising truth about what 'sushi' actually is. T1: sushi does NOT mean raw fish — the raw fish on its own is sashimi; 'sushi' names the seasoned, vinegared RICE (the '-su-' points to vinegar and sourness). T1: nigiri is a hand-pressed finger of that vinegared rice with a topping laid over it. T2: sushi began as a way to PRESERVE fish, not as a fresh delicacy. T2: the ancient method (narezushi) packed cleaned fish in salt and cooked rice and let it ferment for months; the sour, lactic fermentation is what kept the fish edible without refrigeration. T3: in the oldest form the fermented RICE was thrown away — only the preserved fish was eaten (funazushi near Lake Biwa is still made this way). T3: over centuries people began eating the tangy rice too, not just the fish. T4: Edo-period cooks swapped the slow fermentation for a quick splash of rice VINEGAR — instant sourness, no months of waiting. T4: in 1820s Edo (old Tokyo) the cook Hanaya Yohei served hand-pressed nigiri as fast STREET FOOD — the direct ancestor of today's sushi bar. T5: wasabi and pickled ginger aren't only for flavor — both have antimicrobial properties that pair naturally with once-raw fish. T5: the vinegared rice, not the refrigerator, was the ORIGINAL safety technology — acid slows spoilage.
source: Grokipedia checked first — corroborated via en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_sushi, bokksu.com 'Narezushi: The Origins', briandcolwell.com 'A Complete History of Sushi'; funazushi/Kitashina and Hanaya Yohei (1799-1858, nigiri c.1824) per History of sushi.
framing_note: Invert the cliche: hook on 'sushi = raw fish?' and make the vinegared RICE the answer. Accuracy rails: sushi refers to the seasoned rice (raw fish alone is sashimi); nigiri is an 1820s Edo invention, NOT ancient (no anachronism); the oldest narezushi discarded the fermented rice. Payoff rung is T3 (the original sushi threw the rice away and ate only the preserved fish).

name: Koji — the mold behind soy sauce and miso
scope: How a friendly mold turns bland soybeans into the savory backbone of East Asian cooking. T1: soy sauce and miso aren't simply cooked — they're FERMENTED, aged for months from soybeans. T2: the secret worker is koji, a cultivated mold grown on steamed grain or beans — so central to the cuisine it's honored as Japan's 'national fungus.' T3: the mold's enzymes slowly chop the soybean's big, flavorless proteins into small savory pieces — including glutamate, the umami molecule — so time and mold accomplish what no knife or fire can. T4: soy sauce is soybeans plus roasted WHEAT plus salty brine, fermented as a mash and aged; miso is a thick soybean paste fermented with koji-grain — same mold, different texture and time. T5: this is why a spoon of miso or a splash of soy sauce makes almost anything taste 'meatier' — you're adding concentrated glutamate, the very same savory molecule as in dashi. T5: tamari is the wheat-free soy sauce — a byproduct of miso-making, thicker and rounder than regular soy sauce.
source: Grokipedia checked first — corroborated via en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aspergillus_oryzae, mdpi.com 'Japanese Traditional Miso and Koji Making', umamiinfo.com 'Miso', pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov soy-sauce koji studies.
framing_note: Kitchen/prep voice is fine ('you stir in a spoon of miso'). BANNED: the tested answer is never the mold's Latin name (Aspergillus oryzae) or a salt/brine percentage — teach the CONCEPT that fermentation unlocks glutamate. Accuracy rail: soy sauce contains WHEAT (not soy alone); these are fermented, not steeped like tea. Payoff rung is T3 (the mold's enzymes create the umami glutamate — the same molecule as dashi).

name: Kimchi — Korea's living, fermenting dish
scope: The science behind the fizzy, sour, spicy cabbage. T1: kimchi is cabbage preserved by FERMENTATION, not by cooking or canning — it keeps for months and grows more sour the longer it sits. T2: step one is salting/brining the napa cabbage — the salt pulls water out and creates conditions where only the GOOD microbes can thrive. T3: those microbes (lactobacillus, the same family that sours yogurt and sauerkraut) eat the cabbage's sugars and make lactic acid — that's the tangy sourness and the gentle fizz. T4: the fiery RED kimchi we picture is only ~400 years old — before chili reached Korea, kimchi was white and non-spicy (baek-kimchi still is). T5: families once buried sealed pots underground for a steady cool temperature all winter (the kimjang tradition); modern Korean homes keep a dedicated kimchi refrigerator instead.
source: Grokipedia checked first — corroborated via en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kimchi, revolutionfermentation.com '9 Amazing Facts About Kimchi', tastekoreanfood.com 'Kimchi Fermentation & Kimjang'.
framing_note: Matter-of-fact prep voice. Accuracy rails: spicy red kimchi is post-~1600 (chili is a New World plant) and older kimchi was non-spicy; lacto-fermentation is the SAME process as yogurt and sauerkraut. BANNED: no Latin species name as the tested answer — teach the concept (salt selects good microbes; they make lactic acid). Payoff rung is T4 (kimchi wasn't always red or spicy).

name: Tofu — cheese-logic for the soybean
scope: Tofu is dairy-cheese thinking applied to a bean. T1: tofu is made from soy 'milk' — soybeans soaked, ground, boiled, and strained into a creamy white liquid. T2: to turn that milk into a solid block you add a COAGULANT that makes the proteins clump and set — exactly the way cheese is curdled from dairy milk. T3: the classic coagulants are nigari (a bitter mineral salt left from seawater) or gypsum (a chalky calcium mineral) — a small pinch sets a whole pot. T4: how hard you press out the watery whey decides the result — barely set is silky, custard-soft tofu; pressed firm is the block you can cube, fry, or grill. T5: by legend a Han-dynasty prince, Liu An, discovered tofu some 2,000 years ago in China; the delicate skin that forms atop simmering soy milk is skimmed off as yuba (tofu skin), a delicacy of its own.
source: Grokipedia grokipedia.com/page/Tofu checked first (page exists; WebFetch 403-blocked) — corroborated via en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tofu, ift.org 'How Tofu Is Processed', soyinfocenter.com 'History of Tofu'.
framing_note: Prep voice is fine. Accuracy rails: label the Liu An origin as LEGEND, not settled history; tofu is Chinese (Han-era). BANNED: chemical formulas or set-percentages as the tested answer — teach the concept (a coagulant clumps the protein, just like curdling cheese). Payoff rung is T2 (tofu is curdled like cheese — same idea, made from plant milk).

name: Peking duck — engineering shatter-crisp skin
scope: The whole dish is built around one thing: glassy, crackling skin. T1: at the table the prize of Peking duck isn't the meat — it's the paper-thin, shatteringly crisp SKIN. T2: to get there, cooks first separate skin from meat by pumping AIR under the skin so it balloons away from the flesh. T3: the duck is then hung to AIR-DRY for many hours — dry skin crisps in the oven, while damp skin only steams and turns leathery. T4: before roasting, the skin is brushed with a MALTOSE (malt-sugar) syrup — in the heat that sugar browns into the signature mahogany, lacquered sheen (Maillard and caramelization at work). T5: it's an imperial dish perfected in Ming-dynasty Beijing kitchens; the crisp skin is served wrapped in thin pancakes with scallion, cucumber, and sweet hoisin-style sauce.
source: Grokipedia checked first — corroborated via en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peking_duck, nationalgeographic.com 'Peking duck: the complex history', pagefacts.com 'Peking Duck Facts'.
framing_note: Prep/technique voice is the point (the game action is cooking). Accuracy rails: Ming-dynasty imperial origin; the glaze is maltose (malt sugar) and the color is Maillard/caramel, not literal paint. Payoff rung is T2 (air is pumped under the skin to separate it from the meat).

name: Ramen — a Chinese import turned Japanese icon
scope: Japan's most famous bowl started somewhere else. T1: ramen is a wheat-NOODLE soup — the noodles matter every bit as much as the broth. T2: those springy, faintly YELLOW noodles get their bounce and color from kansui, an alkaline (soda) water worked into the dough — plain-water wheat noodles simply won't behave that way. T3: ramen came FROM China — in the early 1900s Japan called it 'Chinese soba' (chuka soba); it is not an ancient Japanese dish. T4: the broth STYLE names the bowl — tonkotsu, for instance, is pork bones boiled so hard and long that fat and collagen emulsify into a creamy, cloudy-white soup. T5: in 1958 Momofuku Ando invented INSTANT ramen — flash-fried dried noodles rehydrated with boiling water — later voted Japan's greatest invention of the 20th century.
source: Grokipedia checked first — corroborated via en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramen, britannica.com/topic/ramen, history.com 'Momofuku Ando creates first mass-market instant ramen (1958)'.
framing_note: Scene-led from the bowl. Accuracy rails: ramen is Chinese-derived (arrived early 20th c.), NOT ancient Japanese; instant ramen is 1958 (Momofuku Ando). BANNED: no chemical name as the tested answer — teach the concept (alkaline water makes the springy yellow noodle). Payoff rung is T3 (ramen is originally Chinese) with T5 (instant ramen) as the fun close.

name: Cantonese cooking — dim sum and the steamer
scope: Cantonese cuisine chases FRESHNESS and turned tea-time snacks into an art. T1: dim sum is a meal of many small SHARED plates eaten with tea; the whole custom is called yum cha, literally 'drink tea.' T2: the plates arrive stacked in bamboo STEAMERS — steaming, a gentle wet heat, is a Cantonese signature because it cooks delicately without masking a food's own flavor. T3: the star dumpling, har gow, has a translucent skin made from WHEAT STARCH (not ordinary flour) — that's what turns see-through and pleasantly chewy when steamed. T4: Cantonese cooking prizes an ingredient's own freshness above heavy sauces — a whole fish is steamed just until done, then finished simply with ginger, scallion, and a splash of hot oil, never drowned. T5: the tradition grew from teahouses along old trade roads in Guangdong, where travelers stopped to rest, sip tea, and nibble — the snacks slowly became a cuisine of their own.
source: Grokipedia checked first — corroborated via en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dim_sum, en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yum_cha, discoverhongkong.com 'Heavenly Kings of Dim Sum', dimsumpalace.com Cantonese guide.
framing_note: Scene-led from the rolling cart and stacked bamboo steamers. Accuracy rails: dim sum / yum cha is Cantonese (Guangdong and Hong Kong); har gow's clear wrapper is wheat STARCH, not rice paper. Payoff rung is T3 (the see-through dumpling skin is wheat starch).

name: Korean BBQ — banchan, ssam and the grill table
scope: A Korean BBQ table is a build-it-yourself meal. T1: the cooking happens AT the table — diners grill strips of meat on a grill set into the tabletop itself. T2: the meat is never the whole meal — it comes surrounded by banchan, a spread of small SIDE dishes (kimchi, pickled radish, seasoned greens) that are refilled for free. T3: you eat it as ssam, a 'wrap': lay grilled meat on a lettuce or perilla leaf, add rice, raw garlic, and a dab of ssamjang (a savory-spicy fermented paste), then fold it and eat in one bite. T4: bulgogi ('fire meat') is marinated before grilling — and Korean cooks often grate ASIAN PEAR into the marinade because the fruit's enzymes tenderize the beef while adding a clean sweetness. T5: the deep savory-spicy base of many Korean sauces is gochujang, a fermented chili-and-soybean paste — and its chili, like kimchi's, only arrived in Korea about 400 years ago.
source: Grokipedia checked first — corroborated via en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ssam, tastekoreanfood.com 'Banchan for Korean BBQ', afar.com 'What Korean BBQ Is and How to Eat It'; pear-enzyme tenderizing (general food science).
framing_note: Prep / at-the-table voice. Accuracy rails: gochujang's chili is post-~1600 (New World plant); the Asian-pear enzyme tenderizing is a real mechanism, not folklore. Payoff rung is T4 (grated Asian pear tenderizes bulgogi).

name: Tempura — the Portuguese gift to Japan
scope: Japan's lacy fried shrimp is a foreign transplant. T1: tempura is seafood and vegetables dipped in a thin batter and deep-fried until pale, lacy, and crisp — light, never heavy or bready. T2: it isn't originally Japanese — Portuguese missionaries brought the batter-frying technique to Nagasaki in the 1500s, and the name likely traces to the Latin 'tempora,' the Catholic fasting days when they ate battered vegetables instead of meat. T3: the trademark lacy, non-greasy crust comes from the batter being ICE-COLD and barely mixed — minimal stirring means little gluten forms, so it fries into a delicate shell rather than a thick, doughy coat.
source: Grokipedia checked first — corroborated via en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tempura, michelin (guide.michelin.com) 'The History of Tempura', aleteia.org 'The surprising Catholic origins of tempura'.
framing_note: A food-history gem. Accuracy rail: tempura is Portuguese-INTRODUCED (16th-c. Nanban trade), NOT indigenous or ancient Japanese; the name traces to Latin 'tempora' (fasting days). Payoff rung is T2 (tempura came from Portugal). The batter-science rung teaches the gluten concept in plain words, no jargon.

name: Stir-fry logic and velveting
scope: Why a good stir-fry needs a plan before the heat comes on. T1: a stir-fry cooks in just two or three minutes, so there's no time to chop mid-cook — everything is cut and measured FIRST, then cooked in a rush. T2: ingredients go into the wok by how long they need — aromatics like garlic and ginger first, then meat, then hardy vegetables, sauce last — so nothing ends up raw or overcooked. T3: crowding the wok is the enemy — too much food at once cools the pan and everything STEAMS grey instead of searing, so cooks work in small batches to keep it screaming hot and dry. T4: restaurant meat is silky because of VELVETING — the raw meat is coated in cornstarch, often with egg white, forming a slick shell that seals in juices and stays tender. T5: a pinch of BAKING SODA in the marinade raises the meat's pH, which keeps its proteins from clenching tight in the heat — that's the real trick behind impossibly tender stir-fried beef.
source: Grokipedia checked first — corroborated via woksoflove.com stir-fry technique guides and general Chinese-cooking food science (velveting = cornstarch/egg-white coat; baking soda raises pH to tenderize).
framing_note: Prep-voice is ideal (the game action IS cooking). Accuracy rails: velveting is a cornstarch/egg-white coat; baking soda tenderizes via pH — a real mechanism, not a myth. BANNED: no exact percentages or gram amounts as the tested answer — teach the concept. Payoff rung is T5 (baking soda's pH trick for melt-tender beef).
